strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: enabling fine-grained, multimodal control (such as identity, voice timbre, and spatial structures) in joint audio-video diffusion models.

The proposed Multi-Modal Control Unit (MMCU) and Dual-Stream Bypass architecture are logically designed to decouple and cleanly inject heterogeneous visual and acoustic conditioning signals into a frozen backbone without hurting pre-trained priors.
Introduces modality-specific guidance scaling, offering users flexible, independent control over visual and acoustic modalities at inference time.

Demonstrates strong quantitative and qualitative performance over existing visual-centric and audio-centric baselines across multiple tasks (talking-head generation, depth/pose-controlled generation).

Comprehensive evaluation that includes both objective metrics (for video quality, audio-visual sync, and structural fidelity) and human user studies, along with thorough ablation experiments in the appendix.
weaknesses: The training dataset (30,000 samples from Hallo3) is heavily human-centric (mostly portraits and talking heads), which may limit the model's generalization to general open-world videos and environmental audio.

Computational overhead of the Dual-Stream Bypass is not fully discussed. Copying transformer blocks at even-numbered layers introduces significant extra parameter count and potential latency during inference.

The algorithmic elements (such as ControlNet-like bypass blocks, cross-attention gating, and classifier-free guidance tuning) are largely combinations of existing techniques adapted to the joint audio-video setup, representing a relatively incremental technical novelty.

strengths: Tackles an important and highly challenging frontier: unified multi-modal controllable joint audio-video generation, combining visual references, voice references, and spatial structure guidance (depth/pose) within a single native model.
The Multi-Modal Control Unit (MMCU) provides a clean, elegant mathematical formulation for handling heterogeneous, multi-modal control signals and masks under a single unified interface.

The Dual-Stream Bypass architecture introduces parallel trainable branches that inject control signals without disrupting the pretrained priors of the joint DiT backbone. Avoiding inter-modality cross-attention within the bypass branches is an effective choice for computational efficiency.
Modality-Specific Guidance Scaling allows flexible, decoupled control over visual identity and voice timbre at inference time without requiring retraining.

The paper features highly thorough and comprehensive evaluations, including extensive objective metrics (VBench, Sync-C/D, Depth/Pose MAE), subjective human evaluation, and direct audio-specific analysis (SIM-o, UTMOS, WER).
weaknesses: The training and evaluation are heavily focused on talking-head/portrait scenarios due to the reliance on the Hallo3 dataset. It remains unclear how well this framework generalizes to more complex, general-domain videos containing multiple moving subjects, diverse camera motions, or ambient/non-speech audio tracks.

The comparison with baselines is slightly biased, as MMControl is built on top of a highly capable state-of-the-art foundation model (LTX-2 19B). Some of the performance gains in visual quality and temporal consistency may stem directly from this massive backbone. Evaluating against a direct control baseline implemented on the same backbone would provide a fairer comparison of the proposed MMCU and bypass design.

The computational requirements are substantial. Although the authors highlight a 12-hour training time as efficient, it utilizes four high-end NVIDIA H200 GPUs for only a small number of optimization steps (7,200) on a 30k dataset. More discussion on the inference latency and memory footprint of deploying a 19B model for real-world controlled generation would be beneficial.

strengths: Addresses an important and highly relevant problem: extending structural (depth, pose) and identity (visual, acoustic) control to native, joint audio-video diffusion transformers (DiTs).

The Multi-Modal Control Unit (MMCU) offers an elegant and unified way to handle heterogeneous inputs (images, audio clips, structures) by temporal concatenation and masking, facilitating easy synchronization.
The proposed Dual-Stream Bypass architecture allows effective conditional injection while preserving the pre-trained generation capabilities of the large frozen DiT backbone.
The introduction of Modality-Specific Guidance Scaling enables decoupled and flexible control over visual and acoustic modalities at inference time without requiring retraining.

Comprehensive quantitative and qualitative evaluations demonstrate significant improvements over existing separate video control or audio-driven generation methods, well-supported by extensive ablation studies in the appendix.
weaknesses: The framework relies on a massive pre-trained backbone (LTX-2 19B), which demands high computational resources (e.g., H200 GPUs) and could limit general accessibility and reproducibility.

The training dataset (30k subset of Hallo3) is dominated by portrait-style or talking-character scenes. Consequently, the applicability of the structural control (depth/pose) to highly complex, dynamic, or open-domain non-human scenes remains less explored.
The manuscript lacks a detailed discussion of failure modes or limitations, such as scenarios where visual and acoustic conditional signals are conflicting or poorly aligned.

strengths: Addresses a highly relevant and timely topic by extending controllable generation to native, joint audio-video Diffusion Transformers (DiTs), overcoming the limitations of previous decoupled/independent control paradigms.

The proposed Multi-Modal Control Unit (MMCU) and Dual-Stream Bypass design are modular and non-intrusive, successfully injecting multi-modal constraints while preserving the robust prior knowledge of the frozen foundation backbone.

The introduction of modality-specific guidance scaling provides great inference-time flexibility, allowing users to independently adjust and balance the visual control (pose, depth, identity) and acoustic control (timbre).

The submission provides thorough quantitative and qualitative results, including evaluations on synchronization (Sync-C/D), visual quality (VBench metrics), and spatial structure (MAE), alongside a robust human evaluation in the appendix.
weaknesses: The manuscript lacks quantitative ablation studies of its architectural choices. It is unclear how different block-insertion frequencies (e.g., every layer versus even-numbered layers) or alternative fusion strategies affect control fidelity and generation quality.

Although Appendix B presents speaker similarity, UTMOS, and WER scores for MMControl, these audio quality metrics are not compared quantitatively against any baselines or ablation models, making it difficult to fully assess the performance of the acoustic control stream.

The decision to omit explicit cross-modal (audio-to-video/video-to-audio) attention mechanisms in the bypass branches is justified by computational efficiency, but the paper does not provide experimental evidence showing whether this omission impacts cross-modal synchronization or joint semantic coherence.

The paper lacks a detailed analysis of the computational overhead (such as parameter count, training/inference latency, or FLOPs) introduced by the bypass branches relative to the base 19B LTX-2 model.

strengths: Presents a timely study on controllable generation for native joint audio-video diffusion models (e.g., LTX-2), addressing a clear gap where prior controllable diffusion works focus either solely on visual or acoustic modalities.

The dual-stream bypass design allows decoupling of the visual and acoustic constraints, which avoids the overhead of cross-modal attention in the control branches and ensures higher computational efficiency during training.
The proposed modality-specific guidance scaling provides great flexibility during inference to adjust control strength independently for visual structure and acoustic timbre.
Achieves high quantitative synchronization scores (Sync-C, Sync-D) and low structural error (MAE on depth maps) compared to the selected baselines.
weaknesses: There is a discrepancy between the general claims of the paper and the portrait-only experiments. Despite claiming a unified framework for joint audio-video generation and leveraging a large foundation backbone (LTX-2 19B), the model is trained and evaluated strictly on a talking-head portrait dataset (a subset of Hallo3). This severely limits the generalizability of the findings to more complex, general videos containing ambient sounds, diverse camera movements, or non-portrait interactions.

Key architectural and implementation details are missing or unclear. For instance, the paper does not explain the native audio representation of the LTX-2 backbone (e.g., latent dimensions, sample rates) and how the bypass branch connects to it. Furthermore, it is unclear how the spatial/temporal dimensions of the masks in equations (2) and (3) are matched and processed by the projectors.

The evaluation lacks comparison against the uncontrolled backbone (LTX-2) itself. It is critical to quantify how much visual quality or temporal coherence is sacrificed when incorporating the proposed control branches.

The claims regarding high computational efficiency lack quantitative support. The paper should provide profiling results (e.g., GFLOPS, parameter size of the bypass branches vs. backbone, inference latency comparison with and without the bypass branches) to validate these assertions.

strengths: Pioneering Exploration: This is one of the first works to study joint multi-modal control (identity, voice timbre, and visual structure) specifically tailored for native joint audio-video Diffusion Transformers (such as LTX-2).

Well-designed Interface (MMCU): The Multi-Modal Control Unit elegantly formats heterogeneous, multi-modal control inputs (images, audio, poses, depth) into temporally synchronized and masked sequences, preventing information leakage and ensuring consistent identity injection.

Modality-Specific Scaling: Introducing independent visual and acoustic guidance scales during inference offers flexible user control over the trade-off between strict structural adherence and generative diversity.

Superior Quantitative and Qualitative Results: MMControl demonstrates strong performance, outperforming existing specialized portrait animation and visual control models on audio-visual synchronization, identity preservation, and depth-control accuracy.
weaknesses: Domain Limitation to Talking Heads: Despite the general title 'joint audio-video generation', both the training set (curated from Hallo3) and all qualitative/quantitative evaluations are strictly centered on talking-head/portrait generation. The paper should explicitly discuss this scope limitation and whether the method can generalize to open-domain video-audio generation (e.g., physical actions, environmental sounds).

Incremental Architectural Novelty: The Dual-Stream Bypass mechanism is conceptually highly similar to established ControlNet or Adapter frameworks, with the main adjustment being the dual visual/audio streams and target-injection layers.

Lack of Quantitative Audio Baselines: While Table S2 presents the audio quality of MMControl, it lacks baseline comparisons (e.g., comparison of speaker similarity and UTMOS against other text-to-speech or talking-head models), making it difficult to fully contextualize the performance.

No Ablation on Cross-Modal Bypass Attention: The authors choose to omit cross-attention between visual and audio within the bypass branches to maintain efficiency. However, there are no experimental ablations justifying how much alignment or performance is traded off by omitting this joint attention.
